To demonstrate, let's use `module list`. `module list` shows all loaded
software modules.

```bash
`r config$remote$prompt` module list
```

```output
Currently Loaded Modulefiles:
 1) vim/8.1   2) intel/20.0u3   3) git/2.49.0   4) miniforge/20251003

Key:
default-version
```

```bash
`r config$remote$prompt` module load espresso/7.2-cuda
`r config$remote$prompt` module list
```

```output
Currently Loaded Modulefiles:
 1) vim/8.1        3) git/2.49.0           5) nv-hpc-sdk/21.3
 2) intel/20.0u3   4) miniforge/20251003   6) espresso/7.2-cuda

Key:
auto-loaded  default-version
```

So in this case, loading the `espresso` module (quantum ESPRESSO, a density
functional theory code), also loaded `nv-hpc-sdk/21.3`. Let's try unloading the
`espresso` package.

```bash
`r config$remote$prompt` module unload espresso/7.2-cuda
`r config$remote$prompt` module list
```

```output
Currently Loaded Modulefiles:
 1) vim/8.1   2) intel/20.0u3   3) git/2.49.0   4) miniforge/20251003

Key:
default-version
```
So using `module unload` "un-loads" a module, and depending on how a site is
configured it may also unload all of the dependencies (in our case it does
not). If we wanted to unload everything at once, we could run `module purge`
(unloads everything).

```bash
`r config$remote$prompt` module purge
`r config$remote$prompt` module list
```

```output
No modules loaded
```

Note that `module purge` is informative. It will also let us know if a default
set of "sticky" packages cannot be unloaded (and how to actually unload these
if we truly so desired).
